articleSummary: As of March 27, 2026, COVID-19 infection can leave sequelae for up to two years post-infection. A 21-year-old male student developed symptoms on 9 March, was admitted 10 March at Gia Định People’s Hospital, then transferred to the Ho Chi Minh City Institute of Tropical Diseases on 11 March; he recovered and was discharged on 19 March. Earlier, in An Giang, an 11-year-old girl died from Neisseria meningitidis group B after presenting with fever, headache, rash and respiratory distress; death occurred despite resuscitation. articleHeadline: El Nino 'Godzilla' Mengancam, Ini Dampak dan Risiko Penyakitnya
articleSummary: Indonesia faces El Niño 'Godzilla,' an extremely strong warming of the equatorial Pacific, potentially with a positive Indian Ocean Dipole, prolonging drought and raising heat across the archipelago, including Jakarta. Risks include heat-related illnesses: heatstroke, heat exhaustion, severe dehydration, heat cramps, acute kidney injury; respiratory infections: ARI, asthma, bronchitis, pneumonia, COPD; haze-related eye/airway irritation with conjunctivitis and reduced lung function, plus cardiovascular risk; waterborne diseases: diarrhea, cholera, dysentery, typhoid fever, hepatitis A; skin conditions: dermatitis, fungal infections, heat rash, bacterial infections; vector-borne diseases: dengue, malaria, chikungunya; nutrition issues: malnutrition, stunting; mental health effects: stress, anxiety, depression. Mitigation requires integrated action: drought planning for the Northern coast of Java, flood preparedness in eastern Indonesia, resource optimization in dry areas (e.g., salt production), and public health education on preventing heat- and drought-related illnesses.

articleHeadline: Molecular evolution and spatial transmission of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus - Nature Communications
articleSummary: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV) from Phenuiviridae shows complex molecular evolution and spatial transmission across East Asia. Analyzing 1942 genomes from humans, animals, and vectors collected 2005-2023 in China, South Korea, Japan, and Thailand, researchers identify two major lineages—L1-Chinese and L2-Japanese-Korean—comprising 13 genotypes (I–XIII). Extensive segment-specific reassortment (212 events; including L1-L1, L2-L2, and L1-L2) and recombination (69 events; 62 in China) shape diversity; the M segment shows markedly higher recombination. Hubei, China emerges as reassortment hotspot; Henan, Hubei, Zhejiang as recombination centers. Bayesian phylogeography traces origin to the Jiangsu-Anhui border region in the 17th century. Two spread networks: L1 terrestrial transmission from Jiangsu-Anhui/Shandong to the Dabie Mountains and Liaoning; L2 marine dissemination with South Korea as a key hub. articleHeadline: Explained: What is Shigella infection?
articleSummary: Shigella infection (shigellosis) caused the death of an 11-year-old boy in Kozhikode, Kerala, last week, with six confirmed and over 30 suspected cases under investigation by the Government Medical College Hospital, Kozhikode. Globally, shigellosis causes about 164.7 million illnesses annually, with 69% of cases and 61% of deaths in children under 5. In six Asian countries, Shigella accounts for about 5% of diarrhoeal cases; among under-5s, incidence is 13 per 1,000 per year. In India, isolation of Shigella from diarrhoeal stools ranges 3-6%. Transmission occurs via contaminated food or water or person-to-person contact, and handwashing can cut transmission by about 70%. Incubation is 1-4 days (up to 8 days for Shigella dysenteriae type 1); symptoms range from mild illness to dysentery with blood and mucus. Hydration is essential; antibiotics (ceftriaxone/cefixime; azithromycin) shorten illness and curb spread. articleSummary: CMNV, a non-enveloped ssRNA virus formerly limited to aquatic animals, is implicated as a potential cause of an emerging human disease: viral anterior uveitis with persistent ocular hypertension (POH-VAU) in China. Disease risk increases with contact frequency/severity with aquatic animals, especially during unprotected handling and consumption of raw seafood. CMNV was found in edible tissues of seafood sold in Chinese markets (fish, shrimp, molluscs) and is globally distributed in farmed and wild aquatic species across continents. Experimental work shows CMNV can raise intraocular pressure and damage eye tissues in mice and infect mammalian cells, including human corneal epithelial cells, causing cell death.

articleSummary: Mpox (monkeypox virus, MPXV) may spread via duikers, small Central/West African antelopes. articleSummary: Symptoms overlap among the common cold, influenza, and COVID-19, but distinctions matter for care. articleSummary: Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SRAG) cases in Ceará total 1,117, according to the Ceará Health Secretariat (Sesa). The current figure is about 1.5% lower than the 1,135 cases reported for the period February 15–March 14 (weeks SE 7–10). SRAG denotes severe respiratory infections that can be caused by viruses such as influenza, coronavirus, rhinovirus, among others. In the latest four weeks, all regions of Ceará have reported SRAG cases, with Fortaleza recording 219 cases, Sobral 124, and Maracanaú 87—the highest subregional counts in recent weeks. The bulletin highlights sustained statewide transmission across regions, without specifying fatalities or laboratory confirmation in the provided excerpt. Data reflect surveillance through mid-March, published March 28, 2026.

articleHeadline: New COVID-19 Variant 'Cicada' Emerges: What To Know And How It's Spreading
articleSummary: BA.3.2, nicknamed 'Cicada', is an Omicron SARS-CoV-2 subvariant with numerous spike-protein mutations. It has been detected in at least 23 countries, with Europe recording up to 30% of recent cases in Denmark, Germany, and the Netherlands, and the United States in at least 25 states (about 0.55% of cases, rising). The first U.S. case was identified in June 2025 at San Francisco International Airport after travel from the Netherlands; subsequent detections occurred in travelers and local samples. Japan, Kenya, the United Kingdom, and parts of Australia have reported cases. Thailand has not confirmed any Cicada infections as of 2026-03-28. Mutations may reduce protection from prior infection or vaccination, but vaccines and boosters continue to protect against severe illness. Transmission is mainly via respiratory droplets; symptoms typically begin 2–5 days after exposure and resemble a cold or flu. WHO and CDC monitor; no call for alarm.

articleHeadline: Kasus Dokter Muda Meninggal Ungkap Bahaya Campak pada Orang Dewasa
articleSummary: Measles in adults is not benign, as a case involving a young doctor in Indonesia demonstrates, with pneumonia and respiratory failure highlighted as major complications. Health expert Tjandra Yoga Aditama of the Indonesian Pulmonary Doctors Association warns that adult measles can be heavy, often more dangerous than in children, and pneumonia is the leading cause of death in measles cases. Indonesia faces a high burden of measles outbreaks (KLB). Vaccination is the most effective prevention: adults typically receive one dose, with two doses in certain risk scenarios, particularly for health workers, travelers to outbreak regions, and other at-risk groups.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Oropouche virus may cause serious effects on pregnancy, according to a study.
articleHeadline: Vírus Oropouche pode causar impactos graves na gravidez, aponta estudo
articleSummary: March 28, 2026 — Oropouche virus (OROV), once confined to the Amazon, is expanding and emerging as a public health threat. A study by Familiar-Macedo et al. in Current Opinion in Virology (2026) shows OROV may have broader risks, especially during pregnancy. Transmission remains primarily by vectors, notably Culicoides paraensis, with possible involvement of Culicoides sonorensis, Culex quinquefasciatus, and some Aedes species, enabling urban and sylvatic cycles. The virus exhibits genetic rearrangements, potentially yielding more transmissible variants. Clinically, OROV infection is often self-limited but can be debilitating and mimics dengue, Zika, and chikungunya, complicating diagnosis without laboratory tests. Crucially, evidence suggests maternal-fetal transmission, placental infection, and adverse pregnancy outcomes when infection occurs in early gestation. Coinfections and potential non-vector transmission further challenge control, highlighting urgent needs for surveillance and research.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Oropouche virus may cause serious effects during pregnancy, study finds.
articleHeadline: Vírus Oropouche pode causar impactos graves na gravidez, aponta estudo
articleSummary: Oropouche virus (OROV) is an emerging urban arbovirus with expanding geographic reach. The principal vector is Culicoides paraensis, but transmission by Culicoides sonorensis, Culex quinquefasciatus, and some Aedes spp. is possible, and non-vector routes—sexual transmission and presence in bodily fluids—raise diagnostics and blood-safety challenges. The virus can rearrange its genome, potentially producing more transmissible variants. Oropouche fever is usually self-limiting but includes fever, headache, myalgia, fatigue, and rash; rare complications include meningitis, encephalitis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome. In pregnancy, first-trimester infection may be associated with miscarriage or congenital malformations; third-trimester infants are often asymptomatic, though risk persists. Placental infection has been observed, signaling maternal-fetal transmission. Coinfections with dengue, Zika, and chikungunya complicate diagnosis and immune responses. Gaps include long-term pregnancy outcomes; need for precise diagnostics, genomic surveillance, vaccines, and antivirals; heightened vigilance for pregnant populations.
notes: 記事サマリーはオロポウシュウイルスの一般的な疫学的特性と妊娠への影響に関する研究知見であり、具体的なアウトブレイク報告ではない可能性がある。発生地域に列挙されたアンゴラはサマリー内に言及されておらず、ガーナのUpper East Regionは地理的位置情報として含まれているが、実際の患者発生状況は不明。継続的な情報収集が必要。

articleSummary: Malaysia’s NPRA has received Envacgen EV71 vaccine NDA for active immunization of children aged 2 months to under 6 years, aiming to protect about 400,000 newborns annually. Envacgen has Taiwan’s EV71 license and Vietnam granted its first EV71 vaccine this year; Singapore and Malaysia filings follow to strengthen Southeast Asia expansion. Enterovirus 71 is a leading cause of hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) in Southeast Asia and can cause paralysis, encephalitis, meningitis, pulmonary edema, hemorrhage, and death. Malaysia lists EV71-related HFMD as a key monitored disease, with 2025 outbreaks rising and severe cases linked to EV71. Phase 3 multicenter trials show 100% efficacy (Poisson regression 96.8%), protective across regional genotypes. Lancet commentary and Vaccines studies emphasize importance for 2–6 month infants, booster durability, and antibodies lasting at least five years.

articleSummary: Whooping cough (pertussis) is an acute respiratory infection caused by Bordetella pertussis, affecting mainly children but also adolescents and adults. Incubation 7–21 days; highly contagious, transmitted by respiratory droplets, especially in closed, crowded settings. Transmission is strongest in the first weeks of symptoms. In Brazil, vaccination with pentavalent or DTP is given in infancy with boosters; maternal immunization during pregnancy (second trimester onward) increases antibodies transferred to the newborn. The disease can cause severe coughing fits lasting weeks, sometimes with a whoop sound; infants under 6 months are at highest risk and may present apnea, poor feeding, or cyanosis. Three clinical phases: catarrhal (1–2 weeks, mild cold-like symptoms and high contagion), paroxysmal (2–6+ weeks, paroxysms of coughing), and convalescent (gradual improvement). Diagnosis combines clinical picture with laboratory tests; treatment includes antibiotics and supportive care. Preventive vaccination remains the most effective control.

articleSummary: Brazil is seeing rising Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SRAG) hospitalizations nationwide, per Fiocruz’s InfoGripe bulletin issued March 27, 2026. All states show a higher SRAG signal in a six-week trend, driven by Influenza A, rhinovirus, and RSV. Rhinovirus is a major contributor, especially among children and adolescents aged 2–14 years. Tatiana Portella of InfoGripe urges high-risk groups—older adults, immunocompromised individuals, and children—to get the influenza vaccine at public health clinics to slow hospitalizations. She also recommends masking in closed, crowded settings and home isolation when symptomatic; if isolation is not possible, wearing a mask to reduce transmission. SRAG incidence and mortality are greatest among young children, mainly due to RSV and rhinovirus; mortality is higher in the elderly, with COVID-19 and influenza A as principal causes. COVID-19 incidence is higher in young children and the elderly; influenza A mainly affects children ≤4 and seniors. Dia D Flu Vaccination Day underway.
